title: Anthropic says Claude Mythos ported a Claude workload to AMD in three days
subtitle: In IPO materials and interviews, Anthropic claims its own model wrote almost all of the kernels needed to run prompt processing on AMD MI355X GPUs — a task that normally takes six to twelve months.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic disclosed during its IPO roadshow — and reiterated after Thursday's Nasdaq debut — that Claude Mythos moved one Claude model's prompt-processing stack onto AMD MI355X GPUs in roughly three days, writing or adapting nearly all of the chip-specific kernels with almost no human help. Co-founder Tom Brown said Anthropic now trains and serves Claude across Amazon Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs and AMD GPUs. The company frames the three-day port as the first visible payoff of using a frontier model to do the systems work that used to pin labs to a single vendor.

The claim is narrower than the headlines suggest. 'Three days' describes a single workload — prompt processing on one Claude model — not a full migration of training, decoding and infrastructure. CUDA is a decade of libraries, compilers and tooling, not just kernels; porting one path is different from running production training on a non-Nvidia stack at scale. Anthropic, in the middle of a roadshow and weeks removed from an AMD commitment of up to two gigawatts of MI450-series Helios systems starting in the first half of 2027, has every incentive to emphasize its independence from Nvidia.

Even granting the caveats, the direction matters. The reason Nvidia commands its margins is the belief that software lock-in is sticky enough that compute budgets have nowhere else to go. If frontier models are capable enough to collapse what used to be year-long kernel-porting projects into days, that belief weakens — not all at once, but at the margin where capex decisions are made. It also lands in a week where Nvidia faces an SEC accounting probe and a China-shipment freeze, feeding a broader narrative that AI silicon is becoming more interchangeable, not less.

A note for learners: the useful question is not 'did Anthropic get off CUDA?' but 'which parts of the stack did the model actually write?' Kernels are the most visible piece; schedulers, collective communication, memory planning and numerical equivalence across hardware are where a real port stands or falls. Read the technical write-ups when they appear, and compare the model-written kernels to a human-tuned baseline on tokens per second and loss curves. That is the measurement that decides whether this is a demo or a commodity shift.
